articles.title: Return to sender: Milotic makes Sunyshore pay
articles.dek: Traded to Violet in Week 5, Milotic scored on an interception and forced the fumble that set up another touchdown in the Falcons’ 33–20 win.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Sunyshore sent Milotic to Violet. Milotic sent the football back 52 yards for a touchdown. Of all the ways the Starseekers could have lost their unbeaten record, arranging delivery of the opposing defensive player of the game is going to be the hardest one to explain.

The cornerback was part of a six-player package Sunyshore traded to the Falcons in Week 5. Before that week was over, No. 89 had intercepted Jolt Vick, forced and recovered Nair Jordan's fumble, and helped turn those mistakes into 14 Violet points. The Falcons won 33–20. You don't need a particularly elaborate calculator to see why his old club might prefer to discuss something else.
I picked Sunyshore. I liked its defense, and I thought it could carry a week without DeZhaun Watzon. Milotic has supplied a fairly pointed review of that argument.

body.speaker: Milotic
body.text: The forwarding address worked.

The first delivery came with 2:54 left in the opening quarter. Violet already led 6–0, and Sunyshore had produced one yard on the first two plays of its second drive. On third-and-nine, Vick threw deep left. Milotic intercepted it and returned it for a touchdown. A conversion later, the Starseekers were down 13 before their offense had made a first down.

It was a dreadful setting for an emergency starter: long yardage, a growing deficit and a cornerback who suddenly had a very personal place in the afternoon. Vick's interception mattered enormously. So did the two runs that left him trying to solve third-and-nine. Sunyshore's opening three drives produced four yards and ended with two punts and Milotic's score.

Violet didn't need a touchdown drive to build a 16–0 lead. Loudred made field goals from 53, 49 and 24 yards, while Zebstrika returned the first two Sunyshore punts 20 and 41 yards. Sunyshore was conceding ground between its defensive series, then asking the defense to defend what was left.
Fourteen points with a familiar name

The Starseekers finally put together a 73-yard touchdown drive, with Scol Alexander finishing from three yards. Fred Whirler then sacked Iron Jugulis on third-and-one. At 16–7, Sunyshore had a stop and a chance to make the game much less strange before halftime.
Milotic interrupted.

At 1:09, Vick completed a short-right pass to Nair Jordan for no gain. Jordan fumbled; Milotic recovered. Two seconds later on the game clock, Iron Jugulis threw short right to Carnivine for a touchdown. Violet's scoring drive was one play. Sunyshore's traded cornerback had supplied the invitation.

The final accounting credited Milotic with three tackles, an interception, a pass defended, a forced fumble, a recovery and a touchdown. Those aren't decorative additions to a winning box score. The two takeaways created the game's most expensive swings, and they belonged to a player the losing team had just chosen to move.

body.speaker: Karson Jones
body.text: We made the trade. We also threw that pass and lost that ball. I'm not going to stand here and turn Milotic's day into an accident. He made the plays.

Vick kept playing. His seven-play response covered 75 yards in 44 seconds and ended with an 18-yard touchdown pass to Fera LaGatr. A missed extra point left it 23–13 at halftime. Later, Vick found MF STOMP for a 21-yard touchdown on third-and-nine, cutting Violet's lead to 26–20 with 50 seconds left in the third quarter.

There was enough offense to win this game. Vick completed 20 of 31 passes for 201 yards and two touchdowns without taking a sack. Sunyshore finished ahead in total yards and first downs, and converted six of twelve third downs. Its line kept the quarterback upright. Its quarterback recovered from the early interception. The rest of the afternoon kept creating new bills.

body.speaker: Jolt Vick
body.text: Third-and-nine, deep left. That's the interception. I don't want it described as something that happened to us. I threw it. But we got back to six points down, and I still thought we could finish it.
The stop that never came
Violet's next drive is why this can't become only a trade story. With the lead down to six, Iron Jugulis took the Falcons 75 yards for the touchdown that restored a two-score margin.

Zack Bear's sack had set up third-and-ten at the start of the fourth quarter. Zangoose ran up the middle for eleven yards. A defense that had just created the down it wanted couldn't finish it. Two plays later, Iron Jugulis found Furret deep right for 26 yards; the quarterback eventually scored from one yard at 4:38.

Furret caught seven passes for 147 yards, including gains of 44, 28, 26 and 24. That was a repeated route to large chunks of the field, not one broken play hidden inside an otherwise quiet day. Zebstrika added a 69-yard punt return in the third quarter, completing a three-return, 130-yard assault on Sunyshore's punt coverage.

body.speaker: Furret
body.text: An upset? We were open. Call it that.
Sunyshore's last drive included Vick's 42-yard completion to Jordan, but ended on an incomplete fourth-and-three pass to Buizel with 4:02 remaining. Violet kept the ball for the rest of the game.

The Starseekers are 4–1. The Falcons are 2–3. Those records will keep Sunyshore above Violet in plenty of arguments about the season, including mine. This particular argument belongs to No. 89: one interception, one forced fumble, one recovery, and a forwarding address Sunyshore won't forget.

art.alt: Milotic wears Violet’s purple No. 89 chest bib against a purple and magenta editorial backdrop.

articles.title: Flock takes the express route
articles.dek: Marshall Flock’s 95- and 93-yard kickoff-return touchdowns turn Mossdeep’s 49–3 victory into a special-teams showcase.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Marshall Flock made Fuchsia pay for scoring. Then he made Fuchsia pay for halftime. Two kickoffs, two touchdowns, 188 yards, and a very clear lesson for anyone preparing to send the ball toward Mossdeep's No. 44: the field is shorter for him than it looks from your end.

The Eclipse won 49–3 and moved to 5–0. Flock, the Swellow listed at halfback, carried only four times. He was still the player of the game. His eight returns produced 314 yards and the two touchdowns that pulled the game away from Fuchsia before Dram Marino needed to spend much of the second half finishing it.

A week after Mossdeep needed a late interception and a last-minute drive to survive at Dewford, this was a welcome change in working conditions. The offense scored five touchdowns. The defense allowed none. Flock supplied two more without asking either unit for another snap.

body.speaker: Marshall Flock
body.text: I like giving the offense a short walk back to the bench.

The first return was especially rude. Fuchsia had just spent fourteen plays moving 46 yards for Clamperl's 40-yard field goal. There were fourth-down yards to earn and repeated tackles to survive. That kick cut Mossdeep's lead to 7–3 with 27 seconds left in the first quarter. The Shadows had finally put something on the scoreboard.

Flock returned the ensuing kickoff 95 yards for a touchdown. Adam Vinathorn's extra point made it 14–3 with eleven seconds left. Fuchsia had used nearly half a quarter to get three points; Mossdeep had answered with seven before the quarter ended. That exchange belongs near the top of any explanation of this game.

The second return came on the opening kickoff of the third quarter. Flock went 93 yards for another touchdown. Mossdeep had led 21–3 at halftime; now it was 28–3 before its offense had run a second-half play. There was no gradual squeeze left to describe. Fuchsia was chasing a game that kept accelerating away from it.

body.speaker: Michael Dorrill
body.text: Marshall changed the score twice without Dram touching the ball. He deserves his name at the top of this one. The rest of us can take a turn below it.
Diggs has his own day

Marino's receivers were hardly spectators. Driflon Diggs caught seven passes for 73 yards and two touchdowns, giving Mossdeep another important story inside a result that will usually be remembered for Flock.

Diggs' first touchdown came on a deep-left throw for 21 yards with 55 seconds left in the second quarter. He had already started that four-play scoring drive with a seven-yard catch to the right. Ninjulio Jones caught a 13-yard pass and ran for four before Marino returned to Diggs. Four plays, three different touches by receivers, and a touchdown before halftime.

The second Diggs score came from six yards with 3:24 left in the fourth. By then the outcome was settled. The contribution still matters for an offense whose injury report now lists Accel BeckhmJr out one week. BeckhmJr caught two passes for 26 yards in this game; Diggs gave the Eclipse substantial receiving production on an afternoon when their usual options were changing.

body.speaker: Driflon Diggs
body.text: Accel's been doing this longer than I have. I don't like seeing his name on that report. I'm happy about the touchdowns. I'd rather have him asking for the next target, too.

Gronkaludon added five catches for 87 yards. His third-quarter touchdown drive was almost comically brief: Marino threw deep left to him for twenty yards, then short right for thirty-one and the score. That is a tight end taking an entire drive for himself, with a quick change of direction between receptions.

Marino finished 18-of-23 for 225 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. Mossdeep needed only four third-down attempts. Fuchsia faced fourteen. I prefer that comparison to a long speech about offensive rhythm: one team repeatedly kept the chains out of the conversation; the other repeatedly had to negotiate with them.

The ground game helped. Ninjaskamara's ten carries gained 94 yards, including the two-yard touchdown that opened Mossdeep's scoring. Jones scored on a seven-yard run early in the fourth. The Eclipse gained 128 yards on seventeen rushing attempts, making the short passing game an option instead of an obligation.
Fuchsia couldn't find a second score

Empoleon attempted 34 passes, completed fifteen and threw an interception to Electric Berry. The Shadows also lost a fumble, and Mossdeep collected four sacks. Clay Rathews supplied two of them. Fuchsia's longest scoring contribution was still the field goal that Flock had answered almost immediately.

Berry's interception came in the second quarter, and his final line included four tackles and a fumble recovery. The defensive player of the game accepted a much quieter kind of attention than the returner.

body.speaker: Electric Berry
body.text: Marshall's the interview. I just wanted the ball back.

There are reasons this victory felt easier than the one at Dewford, and the opponent is among them: Fuchsia fell to 0–5. But ease still has to be produced. Mossdeep did it through clean passing, productive runs, takeaways and a returner who turned two routine restarts into touchdowns. That is a fuller explanation than pointing at the teams' records and closing the notebook.

The Eclipse have scored 203 points in five games. Forty-nine came here. Fourteen of those arrived with Flock carrying a kickoff through the entire scoring argument, and the two distances look almost mischievous beside each other: 95, then 93.

art.alt: Marshall Flock, Swellow No. 44, in Mossdeep magenta and gold on a kickoff return.

articles.title: The Reds survive. The next six weeks just got harder.
articles.dek: Josh Alakazam throws three touchdowns and Foo Warner seals a 24–20 win, but Garshawn Lynch’s six-week absence changes Mt. Silver’s season.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Mt. Silver left Oreburgh unbeaten and considerably less comfortable. The 24–20 victory preserved the Reds' perfect start. The six-week injury listing beside Garshawn Lynch's name changed the part of the season that comes next. One of those facts fits neatly in the standings. The other is going to occupy Connor McLarren for a while.

Lynch caught an eighteen-yard touchdown pass late in the second quarter and gained 44 yards on seven carries. His season rushing total stands at 672. Now the league's leading rusher is out for six weeks, and the Reds must find out how much of their offense travels without him.

It would be a peculiar afternoon to call easy. Oreburgh, now 1–4, led twice in the first half, cut the deficit to one point in the fourth quarter and had the ball twice with a chance to take the lead or win. Mt. Silver needed a fourth-down breakup by Tauros Woodson and a late interception by Foo Warner to finish it.

body.speaker: Garshawn Lynch
body.text: Vibrava got forty-six on the ground! Write that down. I'm annoyed about missing time, obviously, but don't interview me like the rest of them have vanished. Josh can still throw it. You've seen Josh throw it.

Josh Alakazam could, and did. He completed nineteen of twenty-four passes for 230 yards and three touchdowns. Ariados, Lynch and Scep Smith Jr. caught the scoring passes. The Reds' three touchdown drives covered 67, 73 and 73 yards, which is a convincing demonstration of an offense capable of building its own opportunities.

It also explains why this game stayed in their hands after a difficult beginning. Alakazam's first drive ended with Medicham intercepting a deep-right pass on second-and-one. Oreburgh used the next drive to score, with Cryogonal finding Marshtomp from three yards at the start of the second quarter. Mt. Silver had put yards together and received nothing; Oreburgh had turned its chance into the lead.

Alakazam responded with the touchdown pass to Ariados. When Cryogonal found Furret for a fourteen-yard score, Alakazam responded again, this time with the short-right throw Lynch carried for eighteen yards and a touchdown. The game reached halftime tied at fourteen. For all the Reds' reputation, Oreburgh hadn't spent the half behaving like a supporting character.

body.speaker: Josh Alakazam
body.text: I prefer the drives that end with someone else holding the ball. The interception was a poor attempt at that.
Oreburgh keeps the door open

Mt. Silver's first drive of the second half ended with Alakazam finding Scep Smith Jr. for a nine-yard touchdown. That put the Reds ahead 21–14. Then the Miners began using time and smaller gains to work their way back.

A twelve-play drive ended with Marshtomp's 44-yard field goal. On the next Mt. Silver series, Plusico Buress fumbled after an eleven-yard reception and Stunfisk recovered. Oreburgh drove for another field goal, this one from 39 yards. With 2:39 remaining, the Reds led 21–20.

There is an uncomfortable number in the middle of that comeback: Oreburgh converted eight of thirteen third downs. The Reds converted four of six themselves, but their defense kept having to stay on the field. This was the opposite of the previous week's 36–6 win over Lavender, when Mt. Silver had seemed capable of deciding when every part of the game would happen.

The Miners weren't producing the larger offensive total. They finished with 218 yards against Mt. Silver's 319. They were keeping the contest close enough that the next mistake could matter. Buress' fumble mattered. So did the stop Oreburgh made after its second field goal, forcing the Reds to punt with a one-point lead.

body.speaker: Connor McLarren
body.text: The record says five wins. It doesn't say we can afford to give the ball away twice. We had to defend the result after that, and Tauros and Foo made two plays we needed very badly.

At 1:27, Cryogonal threw deep left on fourth-and-four. Tauros Woodson broke up the pass. Mt. Silver took over and gave Vibrava three consecutive runs: five yards left, four up the middle, one right. The first down let the Reds work the clock before Venusaur's 33-yard field goal made it 24–20 with 39 seconds left.

That field goal changed the final task. Oreburgh needed a touchdown. Cryogonal found Furret for seven yards, spiked the ball, then threw short right. Foo Warner intercepted with 24 seconds on the clock and returned it seventeen yards. Alakazam knelt once. Only then could the game be described in the past tense.
A different unbeaten team

Vibrava's nine carries for 46 yards deserve attention beyond Lynch's enthusiastic recommendation. They are actual production from another runner in a game the Reds had to win. That doesn't automatically make Vibrava the answer to six weeks without the league leader, but it gives the discussion a player and a set of carries instead of a vague promise about depth.

Alakazam also spread his nineteen completions across the offense. Gregar Jenings gained 68 receiving yards, Scep Smith Jr. 67, and Tony Gyarzalez added three catches. Mt. Silver has people to involve. The harder question is how the attack changes when opponents can prepare without Lynch at its center.

Oreburgh deserves credit for making this conversation happen under pressure. A one-win team had the ball late against an unbeaten one and forced the favorite to execute. The Miners' last chance ended in Warner's hands; it was a chance all the same.
The Reds are 5–0. Lynch has 672 rushing yards. For the next six weeks, that second number won't move.

art.alt: Mt. Silver crimson helmet with a silver mountain badge beside a football.

articles.title: Saffron scores 48. Lavaridge may keep the zero.
articles.dek: HeeDee Lamb piles up 266 yards from scrimmage, Verrick Brooks records four sacks, and the Psi Corps deliver their third shutout.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Saffron has developed an inconsiderate habit of making its opponents' offensive statistics optional reading. Lavaridge lost 48–0, the Psi Corps recorded their third shutout, and HeeDee Lamb produced enough offense to require a second line on the receipt. I suspect the Inferno would prefer the version with just the final score. It leaves out quite a lot.

Lamb caught ten passes for 204 yards and ran ten times for another 62. He scored once each way. Verrick Brooks collected four sacks. Archiekazam threw four touchdown passes without taking a sack himself. The traveling Psi Corps won the argument early, then spent the rest of the game submitting additional documentation.

This was Saffron's fourth straight victory after the 10–9 opening loss to Vermilion. Yes, I remember that result. No, this is not an invitation to discuss it. The Psi Corps have allowed twenty points across five games, and Lavaridge didn't contribute any of them.

body.speaker: HeeDee Lamb
body.text: Ten carries, ten catches. That's a pleasant way to divide an afternoon. I don't need every touch to look the same.

Lamb's four-yard run to the right opened the scoring with 3:24 left in the first quarter. Saffron had needed five plays to cover 44 yards. The Inferno had already punted once; they would do so seven times before the game ended. Their offense produced three successful third downs in sixteen attempts, which is a long afternoon of walking back toward the sideline.

Saffron didn't need its offense for the second touchdown. Jolteon returned a punt 88 yards early in the second quarter, turning Grubbin's 49-yard kick into seven more points for the visitors. At 14–0, the Psi Corps had touchdowns from a receiver's run and a returner's work. Archiekazam hadn't yet thrown his first scoring pass.

He found Venomoth deep right for fifteen yards at 2:16, giving Saffron its third touchdown before halftime. That throw completed a five-play, 65-yard drive. The efficiency was almost impolite: the Psi Corps were going a long way without giving Lavaridge many opportunities to interrupt.

body.speaker: Archiekazam
body.text: HeeDee makes the next throw easier. They have to account for him, and Venomoth still has a route. I don't mind sharing the explanation.
The zero took work

Lavaridge's best first-half drive lasted seventeen plays and gained 62 yards. It ended on downs. The Inferno had managed to keep the ball, move it and make Saffron defend an extended series. They still went to halftime down 21–0.

That is the part of a shutout that disappears when the score becomes enormous. A defense has to protect it before the margin is comfortable, when a touchdown could still change the game. Saffron did that. The long Lavaridge drive produced more opportunities for a mistake and never got the one it needed.

Brooks made the rest especially difficult. All four sacks of Delphox belonged to the Victreebel wearing No. 52. His season total reached eleven. There are plenty of teams that would enjoy having one player produce that kind of problem; Lavaridge had the less enjoyable task of blocking him.

body.speaker: Verrick Brooks
body.text: Four sacks. I like a number that fits on a leaf.

The defense's success also freed the offense from urgency. Gorebyss made field goals from 48 and 40 yards in the third quarter. Those six points increased the lead to 27–0, and there was no requirement to make every drive spectacular. Saffron could take the points while Lavaridge kept searching for its first ones.

Then the fourth quarter supplied the spectacular again. Archiekazam found Pawmo from a yard out on third-and-one. Lamb caught a thirteen-yard touchdown to the left. Venomoth added an eleven-yard scoring catch with nineteen seconds left. Three touchdown passes in the quarter turned a decisive victory into a number that will be read aloud on every preview show.

The final touchdown followed Pachirisu's interception and 47-yard return. Even after Archiekazam had thrown a late interception of his own, Saffron's defense gave the offense another short assignment. The Psi Corps finished with 383 yards, but they didn't insist on gaining all of them at once.

body.speaker: Delphox
body.text: I had forty-one attempts. I can't tell you there wasn't a chance to do more with them. I can tell you I don't want anyone explaining my afternoon for me.
A team with more than one headline

The temptation is to place Lamb's 266 scrimmage yards above everything else. I won't argue strenuously. Ten catches for 204 yards would have carried a feature by itself; adding ten runs creates a much more troublesome player for a defense to organize around.

But Venomoth caught five passes for 78 yards and two touchdowns. The return unit scored. The kicker made both field-goal attempts and all six extra points. The quarterback had room to throw. Saffron's superiority arrived from too many directions for Lavaridge to fix it with one better matchup.

The Inferno fell to 2–3 after a second straight loss. Delphox finished with 169 passing yards on 41 attempts, and Lavaridge's nineteen runs gained 43 yards. The offense spent too much of the game needing another conversion, another manageable down, another way past Brooks. It found too few of each.

Saffron is 4–1, with a defense that has allowed four points per game. I expect someone will eventually explain why that average is misleading. Until then, Lavaridge's contribution is available for inspection: zero.

art.alt: HeeDee Lamb, Heliolisk No. 11, running in Saffron pink and blue.

articles.title: Four kicks beat the whole Stone offense
articles.dek: Unown goes four-for-four, Disa-Disa-Disa misses the late go-ahead attempt, and Pewter escapes Rustboro with a 12–10 win.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Rustboro found 163 rushing yards, a touchdown and several ways to make its own afternoon miserable. Pewter found Unown. The kicker went four-for-four, including two makes from 52 yards, and the Rockers won 12–10 without scoring a touchdown. If you're looking for a grand strategic explanation, start with the foot.

I'm inclined to like a Stone game built around Philly. Nineteen carries for 97 yards and a touchdown is a perfectly respectable reason. I'm less inclined to admire what Rustboro did with the chances surrounding those carries. Two lost fumbles and a missed late field goal turned a game the Stone could have won into one they'll have to explain.

Pewter's last points came on Unown's 27-yard kick with 5:22 left. Rustboro had time for two substantial drives after that. The first ended with a fumble. The second ended with Disa-Disa-Disa's 40-yard field goal going wide left with 43 seconds remaining. The margin was two. The missed opportunity was larger.

body.speaker: Unown
body.text: Four. It's a good shape.

Unown's first two kicks were the impressive ones: 52 yards in the opening quarter and another 52 in the second. Rustboro had answered the first with a fourteen-play, 82-yard touchdown drive, Philly carrying up the middle from a yard out. The Stone had built the kind of series that makes a running back look like a sensible investment.

Then the offense began spending its success. A nine-play drive gained 34 yards and ended in a punt. Late in the half, Philly lost a fumble on a third-and-ten run, and Swampert recovered for Pewter. The Rockers turned that opening into Unown's 29-yard field goal with four seconds left. Rustboro went to halftime trailing 9–7 despite having scored the game's only touchdown.

body.speaker: Philly
body.text: Ninety-seven yards doesn't cancel the fumble. I know. You can put both numbers in. Just don't act like I spent the other eighteen carries hiding.

It's a fair demand. Philly repeatedly gave Rustboro something to build around. Watchog added 53 yards on five carries, and the team gained more than five yards per rushing attempt overall. The ground game supplied a real advantage. It wasn't enough to rescue every failed throw or every loose ball.

Frosmoth completed ten of twenty-six passes for 93 yards. Pewter recorded eight passes swatted, and Rustboro never threw a touchdown. The quarterback wasn't sacked. That makes protection a particularly unconvincing place to hide the passing performance. The Rockers were disrupting throws without needing to put him on the ground.
The gift, then the repayment

Rustboro received a major chance early in the third quarter when Froslass fumbled a punt return and Solrock recovered. The Stone used the next drive for Disa-Disa-Disa's 32-yard field goal, taking a 10–9 lead at 3:02.

That was an opportunity converted into points, but only three. The distinction became painful when Pewter assembled its fifty-yard field-goal drive across the end of the third quarter and the start of the fourth. Unown's fourth make restored the lead. The Rockers had scored three points four times; Rustboro had no answer that counted afterward.

The Stone's next drive consumed twelve plays and gained 42 yards. On third-and-ten at 2:28, Frosmoth completed a thirteen-yard pass to Glimmet. It should have been the conversion Rustboro needed. Glimmet fumbled, and Tranquill recovered for Pewter. A play that moved the chains instead moved the ball to the other team.

body.speaker: Frosmoth
body.text: Ten completions in twenty-six attempts. That's my number. We had a conversion on the Glimmet play, then we lost the ball. Before that, there were too many throws that gave us nothing.

The defense kept the Stone alive again. Pewter punted, leaving Rustboro 1:49 to find a field goal. Frosmoth completed an eight-yard pass to Huntail on third-and-three. Philly ran for seven. There was a route to a very different ending, and Rustboro had already taken several steps along it.

Then an incomplete pass intended for Diggersby, broken up by Mightyena, left another third-and-three. Nuzleaf ran up the middle and lost a yard to Swampert. Disa-Disa-Disa came on for the 40-yard attempt at 0:43. Wide left. Delcatty's eight-yard run on the next snap used the rest of the game.

body.speaker: Tyler Scarboro
body.text: Our defense kept giving us a chance to finish it. We had the ball after the last field goal, we had it after the fumble, and we had the kick. I can't ask for a fourth ending.

Pewter's offense produced 194 yards and only two third-down conversions. It didn't suddenly become explosive. The Rockers did make every field-goal attempt, recover two fumbles and prevent Rustboro from turning its yardage advantage into a second touchdown. At 3–2, they'll accept that combination without requiring it to look handsome.

Rustboro dropped to 2–3. Armaldo's thirteen tackles and the productive rushing day will survive as good individual work in a losing box score. The decisive comparison is much shorter than that box score: Unown, four-for-four. Disa-Disa-Disa, one-for-two. The last attempt went left.

art.alt: Philly, Gabite No. 63, in Rustboro brown and silver beside a football.

articles.title: Lavender finds two points worth keeping
articles.dek: A 52-yard field goal and two late defensive recoveries help the Wails hold off Hearthome 17–15 and reach their bye at 4–1.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Lavender needed a win it could hold, not a performance it could frame. After the thirty-point defeat at Mt. Silver, the Wails went to Hearthome, made just enough plays, and left with a 17–15 victory. It was untidy and occasionally alarming. It also sent them into their bye at 4–1, which is a rather good place to spend a week considering the untidiness.

The final difference came from two points Hearthome never scored. After Frosmoth's four-yard touchdown pass to Wiglett cut the lead to 17–15, the Haunts tried to tie the game. Vibrava ran up the middle, lost a yard and fumbled; Arcanine recovered for Lavender. The two-point attempt failed with 2:17 left.

Hearthome still got the ball back. Lavender still had to defend the lead. At 1:34, Vibrava fumbled again on a run up the middle, and this time Muk recovered. Diggersby supplied the first down the Wails needed, and Mr. Clanky finished with two kneels. The last two minutes had offered plenty of reasons to worry. Lavender kept the two-point margin through all of them.

body.speaker: Mr. Clanky
body.text: The kneels were my favorites.

That is a reasonable review from a quarterback who had spent much of the afternoon working harder for less. Clanky completed seventeen of twenty-nine passes for 163 yards, threw a touchdown and avoided interceptions. The Wails converted only two of eleven third downs. Their offense repeatedly had to find another way to keep a drive alive or hand the problem back to the defense.

The touchdown pass arrived on fourth-and-four. Trailing 6–0 in the second quarter, Clanky found Beedrill short left for six yards and a score with 1:33 remaining. Lavender had taken twelve plays to travel 68 yards. This was no leisurely response to the early deficit; it required the quarterback to make the conversion on the final available down.

Hearthome had opened the scoring on a fifteen-yard deep-right pass from Frosmoth to Castform at 5:42 of the second quarter. Sunflora missed the extra point. That missed point didn't seem likely to dominate the game at the time. By the fourth quarter, every piece of the arithmetic had acquired a much sharper edge.

body.speaker: Travis Scarboro
body.text: We were going to get asked about Mt. Silver whatever happened here. I'd rather get asked at four-and-one. The fourth-down throw to Beedrill gave us a chance to make that the conversation.
The best minute of the afternoon

After Beedrill's touchdown, the Wails forced a quick punt. Their next drive started with 1:11 left in the half. Seven plays and 58 yards later, Kricketune ran up the middle from one yard for the touchdown that made it 14–6 after the extra point.

Those two late first-half scores carried much of Lavender's day. The Wails had spent the opening quarter without a point and had already punted twice before their first touchdown. Then they put together consecutive scoring drives before halftime. It was the most convincing stretch of offensive football they produced, and it gave the defense something worth protecting.

Diggersby finished with 64 yards on thirteen carries. Carnivine caught five passes for 53 yards; Frosmoth added two catches for 43. Beedrill's six receptions gained only 38 yards, but one ended in the end zone on fourth down. The numbers tell different stories depending on which one you read first. Lavender will happily begin with that touchdown.

Hearthome opened the second half with a twelve-play drive and Sunflora's 39-yard field goal. The Haunts had narrowed the lead to 14–9 and given the Wails a familiar sort of afternoon: every stalled drive threatened to make the next defensive series feel enormous.

Lavender's kicker, Just a cactus, changed the margin with a 52-yard field goal at 5:36 of the fourth quarter. It was his only field-goal attempt. The kick pushed the lead to eight, requiring Hearthome to find a touchdown and a conversion to draw level. The Haunts eventually found the first. The second stayed out of reach.

body.speaker: Just a cactus
body.text: I'm glad they trusted the distance. Fifty-two is a long way to spend watching the ball, even when you're the one who kicked it.

Hearthome's touchdown came after a short, four-play scoring drive. On third-and-four, Frosmoth found Wiglett short left for four yards. There was no spare margin in the conversion itself: four needed, four gained, six points. That brought the Haunts to fifteen and sent Vibrava into the failed two-point attempt.
One more stop was required

Lavender then punted again. This is why the failed conversion can't stand alone as the ending. Hearthome took over with 1:44 left and still had time to win with a field goal. The Wails had to get the ball back, and Muk's recovery did it.

Hearthome's Frosmoth finished with two touchdown passes and no interceptions. Swampert made fourteen tackles. There were performances worth keeping for the Haunts, who fell to 1–4, but the late fumble denied them the chance to turn those performances into a different record.

body.speaker: Frosmoth
body.text: Don't tell me we were nearly good enough. We had the ball with time to win. That's the part I'm going to remember.

Lavender outgained Hearthome 259–206 and avoided a turnover. The Wails also punted five times, struggled on third down and needed a late recovery to protect the result. I don't think anyone who watched should confuse this with a comfortable win. I do think a team recovering from its first defeat is allowed to value the win without first making it beautiful.
The bye arrives with four victories, one loss and a little room to breathe. Clanky's final two plays gained minus-two yards. They were, as he said, his favorites.
